title: HE PREPARED A GALLOWS… BUT ENDED UP PARADING HIS ENEMY
paragraphs:
HE PREPARED A GALLOWS… BUT ENDED UP PARADING HIS ENEMY
When Pride Forces You to Honor the One God Chose
There is a kind of hatred that doesn’t shout… it waits.
It smiles in public, but sharpens knives in private. It builds plans, drafts speeches, rehearses victory… all while pretending everything is fine.
Haman knew that kind of hatred intimately.
He wasn’t just offended by Mordecai. He was consumed by him.
Every time Mordecai refused to bow, something inside Haman cracked a little more. Not because Mordecai attacked him… but because Mordecai would not worship him.

Scripture says in Esther 3:2 that all the king’s servants bowed to Haman, “כִּי־כֵן צִוָּה־לוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ” (ki-khen tzivah-lo ha-melekh) — “for so the king had commanded.”
But Mordecai didn’t move.
No applause. No protest. Just quiet defiance.
And that silence exposed Haman’s soul.
Because pride doesn’t just want recognition… it demands worship.
Haman went home burning. Not satisfied with power, wealth, or influence. One man’s refusal outweighed everything he had.
Be honest… have you ever felt that?
Everything is going right… but one person, one moment, one insult… and suddenly peace disappears.
That’s not a small issue. That’s a heart issue.
And Haman’s heart was already rotting.
So he did what pride always does when it feels threatened… it escalates.
He didn’t just want Mordecai humbled.
He wanted him erased.
Not just him… his entire people.
In Esther 3:6, it says Haman sought “לְהַשְׁמִיד” (lehashmid) — to destroy, annihilate completely.
That’s what unchecked hatred becomes.
It doesn’t stay small.
It spreads.
But here’s where heaven quietly steps in.
Because while Haman was building gallows…
God was building a reversal.
There’s a moment in the story that feels almost accidental, but it’s anything but.
The king couldn’t sleep.
No war. No crisis. Just… restlessness.
So he calls for the chronicles to be read, and suddenly… Mordecai’s forgotten act of loyalty surfaces.
Years earlier, Mordecai had saved the king’s life.
And no one had rewarded him.
Until now.
Right before Haman walks in… ready to ask for Mordecai’s execution.
Timing like that doesn’t belong to coincidence.
It belongs to sovereignty.
The king asks, “What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?”
And Haman… oh Haman…
He thinks it’s about him.
Of course he does.
Pride always assumes it’s the center of the story.
So he paints a picture of glory. Royal robes. A king’s horse. A public parade.
He describes honor with such detail… because that’s what he secretly craves.
Then the words fall like thunder.
“Go at once… and do so for Mordecai.”
You can almost hear his soul collapse.
The man he hates.
The man he plotted against.
The man he refused to tolerate.
Now he has to lift him up.
Scripture records it simply in Esther 6:11:

“וַיִּקַּח הָמָן אֶת־הַלְּבוּשׁ וְאֶת־הַסּוּס… וַיַּלְבֵּשׁ אֶת־מָרְדֳּכַי”
(Vayikach Haman et-halevush ve’et-hasus… vayalbes et-Mordechai)
“So Haman took the robe and the horse… and he clothed Mordecai.”
The hands that built destruction… now dress honor.
The voice that plotted death… now proclaims dignity.
This is what God does.
He doesn’t just stop evil.
He flips it.
Completely.
And maybe this is where it gets uncomfortable…
Because this isn’t just Haman’s story.
It’s ours.
We don’t build gallows out of wood…
But we build them in our hearts.
Resentment.
Jealousy.
Comparison.
Silent bitterness.
Moments where we can’t stand to see someone else lifted because something in us feels overlooked.
Moments where we’d rather see someone fall than face what’s broken inside us.
But God sees it.
Not to shame you…
To save you.
Because pride leads to destruction, but surrender leads to transformation.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is “μετάνοια” (metanoia) — a change of mind, a turning.
Not just feeling bad… but becoming different.
Haman never turned.
That’s the tragedy.
He experienced the humiliation… but not the transformation.
And it cost him everything.
But you… you’re still here.
Which means your story isn’t finished.
Jesus steps into stories like Haman’s… and rewrites them before they end the same way.
Where pride once ruled… grace can take over.
Where hatred once lived… healing can begin.
Where you once resisted… you can now surrender.
Because the cross is the ultimate reversal.
The One who was mocked… is now exalted.
The One who was crucified… is now King.
Philippians 2:9 says, “ὁ Θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσεν” (ho Theos auton hyperypsōsen) — “God highly exalted Him.”
That’s what God does.
He lifts what the world tries to crush.
And He humbles what pride tries to elevate.
So the question isn’t just about Haman…
It’s about you.
What are you building in your heart right now?
And what would it look like to surrender it before God has to tear it down?
Sit with it.
Feel it.
Let it expose what needs to be healed.
Be honest. This hit deeper than expected, didn’t it?
Follow closely if you want daily reminders that don’t entertain your flesh but strengthen your spirit.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… don’t just consume truth, support it being spread.
Join the mission.
This isn’t just content.
This is discipleship.
This is transformation.
This is war for souls.
And you’re invited to be part of it.
Because in the end…
The gallows you build in pride may become the stage where God humbles you… or the place where He begins to change you.
